title: AI that works where your data lives: introducing Zoom AI On-Prem
summary: Regulated enterprises have been locked out of the AI productivity wave. A new deployment model changes that.
body_text: Every major enterprise wants AI, but not every major enterprise can use it the way it's been offered until now. For organizations in data-constrained regions and regulated industries like financial services, government, healthcare, and legal, the calculus has been frustrating: cloud-based AI means data leaves your environment, and data leaving your environment is sometimes a risk you can't accept. While the rest of the market races ahead with AI-generated summaries, real-time transcription, and agentic search, some of these organizations have been left behind — not because they're skeptical of AI, but because no one has given them a deployment model that fits their constraints. CIOs at banks, defense agencies, and hospital systems aren't asking whether they should use AI. They're asking how to use it without violating the data governance policies they spent years building. And until now, the answer has mostly been to wait, pilot something small, watch less-regulated competitors move faster, or cobble together an internal solution that's expensive to maintain. We built Zoom AI On-Prem to end that trade-off. Take control with Zoom AI On-Prem Learn more We bring the AI to your infrastructure Zoom AI On-Prem delivers powerful AI capabilities — beginning with real-time captions and transcription for Zoom Meetings — on your physical servers or private cloud tenant. Your environment, your rules. The Zoom experience your teams know and trust stays intact — the AI processing just happens behind your firewall instead of the Zoom cloud. At launch, that means automatic speech recognition in English, French, German, and Swedish, with more languages coming soon. Meeting summaries, meeting questions, and agentic search are on the roadmap for later this year, with expanding capabilities deployed wherever your data needs to stay. Your teams don't need to learn anything new, either. Zoom AI On-Prem plugs into the same Zoom Workplace experience they use every day — same UI, same workflows, same reliability. The only thing that changes is where the AI processing happens. On-prem without the headaches Here's the part that usually kills on-prem AI projects: maintenance. Managing models, patching software, and keeping pace with a field that reinvents itself every quarter. We took that off the table. Zoom manages integration, updates, patches, and orchestration remotely while you own the environment. Zoom AI On-Prem supports two deployment models depending on your infrastructure. On-premises means Zoom AI models running on your physical servers. Private cloud means those same models running within your own AWS or OCI tenant. Both are deployed through Zoom Node : you add the orchestration platform to your Zoom Workplace license, then enable the AI module. Either way, Zoom handles the orchestration layer, and you get the latest capabilities without managing the AI stack yourself. And the architecture isn't static. It's designed to scale from speech recognition today to meeting intelligence and agentic search later this year. You're not buying a point solution that peaks at transcription — you're getting a deployment model that evolves alongside Zoom AI . Most AI in the market today is cloud-first and document-centric. Zoom's focus is different: conversation-centric intelligence, built around the meetings where real decisions happen, now available wherever our customers need it to live. AI your way, available now Zoom Node is already supporting successful hybrid deployments with highly regulated organizations — enterprises that face data residency mandates, sovereignty requirements, and compliance frameworks that dictate exactly where infrastructure can run. Now, we're extending that same flexibility to key AI processing. Organizations that have trusted Zoom Node to meet their strictest infrastructure requirements can now add AI capabilities that respect those same boundaries, deployed the same way, in the same environments where their data already lives. For years, regulated enterprises have faced a false binary: AI-powered productivity or enhanced data control. Zoom AI On-Prem provides a platform to support both. Available June 22, 2026, through the Zoom Node add-on to paid Zoom Workplace plans. Deployment is supported through our enterprise sales team and Zoom Professional Services. Take control with Zoom AI On-Prem Learn more

title: How to Find the One Fact That Decides a Case in Medical Records
summary: The fact that decides a claim is often on a single page of a massive file. Here is how AI-powered medical record review helps teams surface it faster.
body_text: Most disputed claims and injury cases do not turn on brilliant legal argument. They turn on whether someone found the one page, in a record set of thousands, that changes the story. Every experienced legal nurse consultant and litigator knows this. The frustrating part is that finding that page has almost nothing to do with skill and almost everything to do with whether a reviewer happened to be alert on hour six of a page-by-page read . Diligence does not scale. A 4,000-page record set does not get 4,000 pages of equal attention, no matter what the billing entries say. Illustrative Diligence doesn't scale across a 4,000-page read Hour 1 96% Hour 2 81% Hour 3 66% Hour 4 48% Hour 5 33% Hour 6 20% Effective attention per page as one reviewer moves through a large record set. The decisive page is just as likely to land in hour six as in hour one. Below are three composite cases, drawn from patterns we see constantly in medical-legal review , that show where the needle tends to hide and what it takes to surface it. Details have been changed and combined; the record problems are real. Case 1: The Herniation That Predated the Crash The setup A rear-end collision, moderate property damage. The plaintiff, a 42-year-old warehouse lead, claimed an L4-L5 disc herniation caused by the crash, with a demand built on an MRI taken five weeks post-accident, ongoing pain management, and a surgical recommendation. Nine treating providers. Roughly 2,800 pages of records produced across multiple productions, in no particular order. Where the needle was hiding The records from each provider were internally chronological, but nobody reviews nine providers as one timeline. They review them as nine stacks. And in stack form, the story held up: crash, ER visit, orthopedic referral, MRI, herniation. Merged into a single unified chronology , the story broke. A chiropractic clinic, one of the nine providers, had produced records going back further than anyone had focused on. Sorted into the master timeline , a treatment note from 14 months before the collision described “chronic low back pain radiating to the left leg” and referenced an outside imaging report. That reference pointed to an MRI that was never produced in any of the nine record sets. The chronology flagged it as a cited-but-missing document . What the expert did with it The reviewing nurse consultant pulled the thread. A targeted records request for the referenced imaging came back with a pre-accident MRI showing the same L4-L5 herniation, nearly identical in description to the post-accident study. Why it made the difference Causation collapsed from “the crash herniated the disc” to, at most, “the crash may have aggravated a documented pre-existing condition.” The case settled at a fraction of the original demand. The decisive fact was always in the produced records; it was just sitting in the wrong stack, 14 months away from where anyone was looking. Case 2: The Six Weeks That Were Billed but Never Produced The setup A workers’ compensation claim : a shoulder injury attributed to a lifting incident at a distribution center. The claimant’s condition worsened sharply about two months post-injury, escalating from conservative care to a surgical repair. The carrier’s file contained around 1,900 pages of records plus itemized billing. Where the needle was hiding Nothing in the medical records themselves looked wrong. The gap only appeared when the records were reconciled against the billing . Cross-referencing every billed encounter against its corresponding clinical record surfaced a mismatch: an urgent care facility had billed for two visits during a six-week window from which no treatment records had been produced at all. On a page-by-page read, a reviewer sees the records that exist. Nobody sees the records that are absent , because absence doesn’t have a page. What the expert did with it The nurse reviewer flagged the gap, and counsel requested the missing urgent care records. When they arrived, the first visit note told a different story: the claimant had presented after a weekend recreational softball game, reporting acute shoulder pain after “diving for a catch.” The second visit documented worsening symptoms, still with no mention of the workplace incident. Why it made the difference The sudden clinical deterioration now had a competing explanation, an intervening event squarely inside the unexplained window. The claim didn’t vanish, but apportionment changed entirely, and the surgical costs were no longer presumptively attached to the workplace injury. The make-or-break fact wasn’t in the file. The make-or-break fact was that the file had a hole , and the hole was only visible when billing and records were laid side by side. Case 3: The Progress Note That Existed Twice The setup A hospital negligence matter involving an alleged delayed response to a patient’s deterioration overnight. Roughly 4,600 pages: physician notes, nursing flowsheets, medication records, and multiple overlapping productions from the hospital as discovery dragged on. Where the needle was hiding Overlapping productions mean duplicates, and most review workflows treat duplicates as noise to be skipped. Deduplication done properly does the opposite: it compares near-identical documents to each other. That comparison surfaced two versions of the same overnight progress note, identical in header, author, and almost all content, except that the later-produced version contained an added sentence stating the physician had been “notified of vitals and evaluated the patient at bedside” during the critical window. The metadata told the rest. The amended version carried an electronic signature timestamp from three days after the adverse event, with no amendment annotation. What the expert did with it The consultant lined up the two versions against the nursing flowsheets and the audit trail counsel subsequently requested. The flowsheets recorded escalating abnormal vitals with no corresponding physician entry during the window in question. The audit trail confirmed the note had been edited after the outcome was known. Why it made the difference The case stopped being a debate between experts about clinical judgment and became a case about the reliability of the record itself. An unannotated late amendment, discovered because two “duplicate” pages weren’t actually duplicates, reframed everything the defense filed afterward. It settled before depositions concluded, with the spoliation exposure hanging over every subsequent filing. The Pattern Across All Three None of these facts required unusual medical insight to interpret. Any competent nurse consultant or attorney, handed the right page, sees the significance in seconds. Case Where the fact hid Why linear review misses it What surfaced it Pre-existing herniation One provider's stack, 14 months before the crash Nine providers get read as nine stacks, never one timeline A unified chronology that flagged a cited-but-missing MRI Six unproduced weeks In records that were never produced at all A reviewer sees the pages that exist, not the ones that are absent Reconciling every billed encounter against its clinical record The altered note Inside its own near-duplicate, added after the fact Duplicates get skipped as noise instead of compared Deduplication that compares near-identical pages, plus the audit trail The hard part was never the judgment. It was the exposure. A pre-existing condition hides in provider sequence. A missing record hides in what was never produced. An altered note hides inside its own duplicate. Linear page-by-page review is structurally bad at all three, because each one only becomes visible when the record set is treated as a single organized whole : one unified timeline, every bill reconciled to a record, every near-duplicate compared instead of skipped. That is the work InQuery’s structured review is built to do: sort the chaos, reconstruct the timeline, flag the gaps, and put the anomalies in front of the expert. The expert still reads the page, weighs the fact, and makes the call. We just make sure the page gets found. If your cases involve record sets big enough that “we reviewed everything” is more hope than fact, that’s exactly the situation this process exists for. Reviewing record sets too big to trust "we read everything"? See how InQuery's claim file review reconstructs the timeline, reconciles the billing, and puts the anomalies in front of your expert. Request a sample review Frequently Asked Questions How is this different from an AI medical record summary? A summary condenses what a document says. Finding the decisive fact is a different job: it means reconstructing one timeline across every provider, reconciling bills against records, and comparing near-duplicates so anomalies surface. InQuery pairs that structured review with a human QA layer, so the output is both organized and defensible. Does structured review actually help on very large record sets? The larger the file, the more the odds favor it. A decisive page is easy to miss in a 4,000-page read and hard to miss when the set is sorted, indexed, and cross-referenced as one whole. Volume is where linear review breaks down and where structure pays off most. What kinds of problems does this catch that a page-by-page read misses? The three failure modes in this article: records that were never produced , billing-to-record mismatches, and altered or late-amended notes. Each is invisible in a single stack and only appears when the record set is organized, reconciled, and deduplicated against itself. How do I try this on one of my own cases? Send a representative file and we will show you what the review surfaces, with each finding traced back to its source page. You can request a sample review and see the output on a real record set before committing to anything. The cases above are composites based on recurring patterns in medical-legal record review. Identifying details are fictional; the failure modes are not.

title: 15 hábitos para mejorar tu seguridad al conducir
summary: Desde cambiar de ruta hasta mantener tu auto limpio y ordenado, te dejamos 10 consejos para mejorar tu seguridad al conducir.
body_text: Conducir se puede volver una tarea demasiado monótona, ya lo decía el poeta Homero S: “acelero, freno claxon; claxon claxon recto”. Pero tal vez no sabías que en muchas ocasiones conducimos por puro instinto , sin estar realmente conscientes de los que estamos haciendo. Conducir de forma instintiva puede ponernos en riesgo pues aumenta la posibilidad de tomar una decisión errónea frente al volante. Al manejar de esta forma se pierden muchos detalles del camino y el riesgo de tener un accidente aumenta demasiado. En este artículo te queremos compartir algunos consejos de buenas prácticas para reducir la monotonía al conducir , mejorar tu seguridad y de paso disminuir el estrés frente al volante. Cambia de ruta constantemente Al conducir en la ciudad es muy común que las personas tengan un ruta establecida , de su casa al trabajo y del trabajo a su casa. Pero una buena idea es cambiar este hábito al menos una vez por semana. Los beneficios son simples pero muy significativos. Al cambiar de ruta por obviedad sabrás nuevos caminos hacia tu destino, algo muy útil en ciudad tan transitadas en México. Además, una nueva ruta mantiene al cerebro alerta sobre los obstáculos que se presenten. Mantén una posición correcta de tus manos en el volante Casi todas las escuela de manejo, aconsejan colocar las manos separadas en el volante y en el extremo superior. Para ponerlo más sencillo, pensando que el volante es un reloj, las manos deberían estar en el 10 y el 2. Al aprender a conducir siempre nos recomiendan abrir un poco este ángulo. Poniendo el mismo ejemplo del reloj, las manos deberían ir a las 9 y las 3. Los argumentos son muchos pero el más importante es que de esta forma se puede maniobrar el volante con más naturalidad . Aumenta el espacio entre vehículos Muchos especialistas recomiendan a los conductores manejar como si tuvieran un auto con unas dimensiones más grandes. Con un poco de práctica es sencillo imaginar que nuestro auto es un volumen más grande. La razón es sencilla, al tener esta dimensión en la mente se conduce con mayor precaución y por instinto se aumenta las distancias con otros autos , se anticipan con más tiempo las vueltas y se evitan movimiento abruptos. El resultado es una mayor seguridad al conducir. Mira más adelante En la monotonía de la conducción es fácil concentrarnos en la parte delantera del cofre del auto y prestar poca o nula atención al camino frente a nosotros. Es de vital importancia mantener nuestra atención unos 5 o 7 metros adelante en el camino, pues dependiendo la velocidad, podemos estar en ese punto en fracciones de segundo. Por eso, lo más recomendable es que prestes atención al camino delante de tu auto, incluso realizar unas miradas repentinas a unos 15 o 20 metros delante tuyo. Presión de los neumáticos El funcionamiento óptimo de los neumáticos es de vital importancia en la seguridad de un automóvil, pues es el elemento que tiene contacto con el asfalto del camino. Por esto, un buen hábito es revisarlos de forma semanal para detectar pinchazos o cuarteaduras. De igual forma es importante realizar la alineación y el balanceo. ¿Quieres comprar tu auto? , en Nexu te ofrecemos un esquema de financiamiento personalizado para que obtengas el mayor beneficio. Conoce cómo trabajamos y cotiza tu financiamiento en www.nexu.mx. Cuida y utiliza los retrovisores La vida del conductor está en los retrovisores reza un dicho muy conocido en los profesionales del volante. Y no es para menos, los retrovisores nos permiten ver todos los objetos que tenemos atrás y si se acerca o alejan de nosotros. En primer lugar debemos cuidarlos y mantenerlos funcionando correctamente . Debemos evitar que los espejos se rompan o tengan un exceso de opacidad o bien nos estén bien ajustados. Te puede interesar: ¿Sabes cuál es la posición correcta del retrovisor y espejos laterales? Cambio de carril y punto ciego Al cambiar de carril o bien adelantar a un auto, necesitamos confiar mucho en los retrovisores para asegurarnos de que el camino está libre. Sin embargo, existe un punto ciego en el auto , en el cual tanto los laterales como el retrovisor no alcanzan a ver. Al cambiar de carril o adelantar vigila bien que el camino esté despejado y por supuesto utiliza las direccionales para alertar a otros conductores. Cabe mencionar que en la actualidad los asistentes de conducción te alertan sobre cualquier objeto en el punto ciego pero aún cuando la alerta no se active, cerciórate antes de cambiar de carril. Direccionales Debido a su importancia y a la costumbre de muchos conductores de no utilizar las direccionales, es necesario hacer hincapié en este punto. Las direccionales advierten a los demás conductores del próximo movimiento de nuestro vehículo y previenen muchos percances. Además de los conductores, peatones y ciclistas pueden advertir nuestros movimientos con este dispositivo dentro del auto. Cuida el movimiento de tus manos Al conducir de vez en vez vamos a necesitar voltear a los lados. Siempre que regresemos rápido la vista al camino, esta acción no debe ser un problema, el riesgo sucede cuando al girar la cabeza también giramos el volante. Es un hábito que nos es tan común pero para las personas que lo practican puede ponerlos en serios riesgos de sufrir un accidente. Por ejemplo, cuando vamos a girar hacia algún lado, muchos conductores deben voltear para eliminar el punto ciego, lo cual los pone en riesgo. Si detectamos que somos que tenemos este hábito, deberemos corregirlo de inmediato. Los cambios ayudan Muchas personas prefieren un vehículo manual sobre uno automático , por la mayor interacción con el auto al tener que realizar los cambios. Una ventaja extra es que, este constante movimiento evita la monotonía al conducir y te mantiene alerta. Limpieza en el interior del auto En un artículo pasado te dimos una guía para limpiar el interior del auto y toma especial relevancia también en la seguridad al conducir pues en una fuerte frenado, los objetos dentro del vehículo pueden convertirse en un proyectil. Hay mucho casos de accidentes ocasionados por conductores que intentaban recoger su celular u otro objet o que se había caído por el movimiento natural del vehículo. Es por eso que mantener un auto limpio y ordenado mejora tu seguridad al conducir. Platicar o cantar Así como lo oyes, cantar mientras conduces además de reducir el estrés en general, te permite estar más atento al conducir. Existen alguna música "peligrosas" par conducir pues se considera que acelera nuestro ritmo cardiaco y con ello nuestra disposición a acelerar. Aunque no está 100% comprobada esta teoría, siempre es mejor elegir música tranquila y no demasiado relajante para evitar quedarnos dormidos. Ropa al conducir La ropa afecta la forma en cómo conducimos así lo sostienen varios estudios y aunque puede estar un poco a debate, es claro que nunca debes utilizar suelas muy gruesas o tacones para conducir. Tampoco es recomendable utilizar roba muy abultada o apretada pues reduce nuestro tiempo de reacción frente a una situación repentina. Sueño al conducir Tener sueño mientras se conduce es muy peligroso por razones obvias. La falta de concentración en el camino puede provocar un accidente en nosotros o los demás conductores. Existen muchas formas de evitar el sueño mientras conducimos como platicar con tu copiloto, masticar un chicle o simplemente descansar un poco antes de continuar tu camino. Opacidad espejos La falta de claridad en el camino por la opacidad en el parabrisas, ventanas o espejos laterales es muy riesgoso para un conductor. Hay mucho que hacer para evitar el paño en los vidrios y espejos del auto. Podemos utilizar la calefacción, antiadherentes o simplemente abrir la venta. Te puede interesar: Consejos para conducir bajo la lluvia ¿Qué te parecieron estos consejos para mejorar tu seguridad al conducir? Si tienes algún otro tip, te invitamos a que nos dejes un comentario.
